items.prompt: What does the strangler fig pattern actually replace a big-bang rewrite with?
choices: A faster rewrite, done in half the time
A routing facade that sends traffic to old or new system per route, migrated incrementally with both systems live
A tool that automatically rewrites legacy code into new code
A freeze on new features until the rewrite finishes
items.explanation: The pattern's core mechanism is a facade deciding, per route, which system answers — allowing migration one capability at a time instead of one all-or-nothing cutover, with both systems running simultaneously the whole time.
items.reference:
Client→Facade→Old or new, per route

Why: the facade is what lets old and new coexist, so migration happens one route at a time instead of one all-or-nothing cutover.

items.prompt: A team says they're 'doing a strangler fig migration' but their plan is: build the whole new system in a branch, then swap it in on one deploy. Is that actually the strangler fig pattern?
choices: Yes — any eventual replacement counts
No — the defining feature is incremental migration behind a facade with both systems live, not a single swap regardless of how the new system was built
Yes, as long as the new system is better code
No — it only counts if it takes over a year
items.explanation: A single swap, even of a well-built replacement, is a big-bang cutover in disguise — it carries the same all-or-nothing risk the pattern exists to avoid. The name applies specifically to gradual, facade-mediated migration.
items.reference:
Client→Facade→Old or new, per route

Why: the facade is what lets old and new coexist, so migration happens one route at a time instead of one all-or-nothing cutover.

items.prompt: Why is the plant metaphor ('strangler fig') actually apt for this pattern, beyond just being a memorable name?
choices: It isn't apt — it's purely a marketing name
The fig grows to full independence around the host while the host stays alive, and only afterward does the host get removed — matching new-system-grows-around-old-while-both-run, retire-old-last
It's apt because figs grow very quickly
It's apt because the fig and the host tree are the same species
items.explanation: The biological process is a precise structural match: the fig never requires the host to stop functioning while it grows, and removal of the host happens only after the fig is already self-sufficient — exactly the sequencing a good migration follows.
items.reference:
Client→Facade→Old or new, per route

Why: the facade is what lets old and new coexist, so migration happens one route at a time instead of one all-or-nothing cutover.

items.prompt: What is the facade's job in a strangler fig migration?
choices: Rewriting legacy logic into a modern style automatically
Deciding, per request, whether the legacy or new system answers — invisibly to the client
Storing all application data during the migration
Running automated tests against the legacy system
items.explanation: The facade is a thin routing layer, not a logic-rewriting tool or a data store. Its only job is deciding which backend answers a given request, in a way the client never has to know about.
items.reference:
PieceJob
FacadeRoutes each request, old or new
LegacyKeeps running, unmodified
NewGrows one route at a time

Why: the client never sees which system answered — that decision lives entirely in the facade.

items.prompt: A developer adds `if (useNewCheckout) { ... } else { ... }` checks directly inside the client's checkout page component. Is that equivalent to a strangler fig facade?
choices: Yes — same effect, different location
No — it scatters the routing decision into client code instead of centralizing it in one facade, making it harder to change or roll back consistently
Yes, as long as the flag is stored in a config file
No, but only because client code can't call two systems
items.explanation: Centralizing the decision in one facade is what makes flipping a route, or rolling one back, a single, consistent, testable change. Scattering the same check across client code means every scattered copy has to be found and flipped in sync — exactly the fragility the pattern is designed to avoid.
items.reference:
PieceJob
FacadeRoutes each request, old or new
LegacyKeeps running, unmodified
NewGrows one route at a time

Why: the client never sees which system answered — that decision lives entirely in the facade.

items.prompt: What is the core risk a big-bang rewrite carries that a strangler fig migration avoids?
choices: Big-bang rewrites are always written in a worse programming language
All the value is delivered at once, on one cutover, made by people who may not remember every rule the old system encodes — with no small, reversible steps along the way
Big-bang rewrites can't use version control
There is no real difference in risk between the two approaches
items.explanation: A single cutover concentrates all the risk into one event, with no intermediate checkpoints and no way to isolate a failure to a small piece. A strangler fig migration spreads the same total risk across many small, independently reversible steps.
items.reference:
Big-bang

0% value until cutover, 1 huge rollback

Strangler fig

Value each week, small rollback per route

Why: small, reversible bets beat one large irreversible one, especially when the people who understand the old system's edge cases are limited.

items.prompt: A big-bang rewrite that ships successfully on its first attempt still has one structural downside compared to a strangler fig migration that took the same total calendar time. What is it?
choices: It has none — a successful rewrite is strictly better
Customers saw zero improvement for the entire duration, and the team had no real production feedback until the very end
It always costs more money regardless of outcome
It can't be tested before shipping
items.explanation: Even a rewrite that eventually succeeds still delayed all value delivery to the final cutover and got no real production signal on any of its assumptions until then — a strangler fig migration gets both value and feedback continuously, which is a structural advantage independent of whether the rewrite 'worked.'
items.reference:
Big-bang

0% value until cutover, 1 huge rollback

Strangler fig

Value each week, small rollback per route

Why: small, reversible bets beat one large irreversible one, especially when the people who understand the old system's edge cases are limited.

items.prompt: If migrating one route behind a facade exposes a bug in the new system, what's the rollback compared to a big-bang rewrite's rollback?
choices: Both require the same amount of rollback work
The facade migration only needs that one route flipped back; the big-bang rewrite has no equivalent small move — the only rollback is reverting the entire cutover
Neither approach can be rolled back once shipped
The big-bang rewrite is actually easier to roll back because it's one deploy
items.explanation: Per-route rollback in a facade migration is a single, small, targeted change. A big-bang rewrite has no unit smaller than 'the whole cutover' to roll back — a bug found anywhere forces reverting everything, usually under time pressure.
items.reference:
Big-bang

0% value until cutover, 1 huge rollback

Strangler fig

Value each week, small rollback per route

Why: small, reversible bets beat one large irreversible one, especially when the people who understand the old system's edge cases are limited.

items.prompt: Between `GET /products` (read-only, high traffic) and `POST /orders` (writes money, lower traffic), which should typically migrate first?
choices: POST /orders, because it matters more to the business
GET /products — it's the cheapest way to prove the facade works, with a failure mode that's merely embarrassing rather than financially damaging
Whichever route has fewer lines of code
They should always migrate at exactly the same time
items.explanation: Migration order should track blast radius, not business importance. A read-only route proves the facade and the new system's basics on real traffic without risking money if something goes wrong — earning confidence before tackling the riskier write path.
items.reference:
Migrate early

Read-only, reversible, cheap failure

Migrate late

Writes money/state, costly failure

Why: order should track blast radius, not the alphabet or business importance.

items.prompt: A team migrates their dozen routes in alphabetical order. What's the problem with that?
choices: There's no problem — alphabetical order is as good as any other
Alphabetical order has no relationship to risk or blast radius, so a high-stakes route can end up migrated before the facade has proven itself on safer traffic
Alphabetical order is illegal under most style guides
It only works for routes starting with letters A through M
items.explanation: Order should be chosen deliberately by risk, not by an arbitrary sort. Alphabetical order can just as easily put `POST /orders` before `GET /products`, migrating the highest-blast-radius route before the facade has any track record at all.
items.reference:
Migrate early

Read-only, reversible, cheap failure

Migrate late

Writes money/state, costly failure

Why: order should track blast radius, not the alphabet or business importance.

items.prompt: At a high level, what does 'shadowing' a route mean during a migration?
choices: Hiding the route from monitoring until it's fully migrated
Calling both the legacy and new system on real traffic, returning the legacy answer to the client, and recording whether the new system agreed
Copying the legacy system's database into the new system
Running the new system only in a staging environment, never on real traffic
items.explanation: Shadowing forwards real production traffic to the new system for comparison purposes only — the client always gets the legacy answer, so a bug in the unproven new system can never reach a real user during this stage.
items.reference:
🔁 Both systems called, legacy answer returned to client, agreement logged

Why: shadowing gathers evidence about the new system's correctness before any customer depends on it.

items.prompt: During shadowing, the new system throws an error on a request the legacy system handled fine. What should happen from the client's point of view?
choices: The client sees the error, since it's real feedback about the new system
Nothing changes for the client — they still get the legacy system's answer, and the error is just logged as a mismatch
The request should fail entirely, since one of the two systems errored
The client should be shown both answers and asked to pick
items.explanation: Shadowing exists precisely so the new system's failures stay invisible to real users while still being captured as data. The client only ever sees the legacy system's answer during this stage — that's what makes it safe to shadow with genuinely unproven code.
items.reference:
🔁 Both systems called, legacy answer returned to client, agreement logged

Why: shadowing gathers evidence about the new system's correctness before any customer depends on it.

items.prompt: Why is shadowing considered stronger evidence than passing a test suite before migrating a route?
choices: It isn't — a good test suite is always sufficient on its own
Shadowing checks agreement against real, unfiltered production traffic, which exercises cases a test suite's authors may not have anticipated
Shadowing runs faster than a test suite
Test suites can't be automated, but shadowing can
items.explanation: A test suite only covers cases someone thought to write. Shadowing is checked against whatever traffic production actually sends, which reliably surfaces edge cases (unusual inputs, rare data shapes) that nobody wrote a test for.
items.reference:
🔁 Both systems called, legacy answer returned to client, agreement logged

Why: shadowing gathers evidence about the new system's correctness before any customer depends on it.

items.prompt: What is the facade's core data structure, and what does flipping one entry in it actually do?
choices: A cache of legacy responses — flipping an entry clears the cache
A lookup table mapping route to target system — flipping an entry is the entire mechanism of migrating that route, with no client change or redeploy needed
A queue of pending migrations processed one per day
A copy of the legacy system's source code, edited in place
items.explanation: The routing table is deliberately the single source of truth for 'who owns this traffic right now.' Changing one entry is a config-level change, not a code change — no client update, no DNS change, no legacy redeploy required.
items.reference:
{"GET /products": "new",
 "POST /orders": "legacy"}

Why: the routing table is the single source of truth — flipping one entry is the whole migration mechanism for that route.

items.prompt: `GET /products` is flagged 'new' and `POST /orders` is flagged 'legacy' in the routing table at the same moment. Is that a valid state?
choices: No — all routes must migrate together or the system is inconsistent
Yes — different routes can be served by different systems simultaneously; that's the entire point of routing per-route instead of per-deploy
No — the facade can only forward to one backend at a time
Yes, but only if both routes belong to the same HTTP method
items.explanation: Per-route routing is exactly what lets a low-risk route (read-only catalog) run on the new system while a high-risk route (order writes) stays on legacy until it has earned that move separately.
items.reference:
{"GET /products": "new",
 "POST /orders": "legacy"}

Why: the routing table is the single source of truth — flipping one entry is the whole migration mechanism for that route.

items.prompt: At 2am, a route flagged 'new' turns out to have a bug. What is the actual incident response?
choices: Redeploy the legacy system to take back the traffic
Flip that one routing table entry back to 'legacy' — a config change to one line, not a code revert or redeploy
Roll back every already-migrated route, not just this one
Take the whole site offline until a fix ships
items.explanation: Because routing decisions live in one small table, the incident response is scoped to exactly the affected route: flip its entry back. Nothing else changes, and no deploy of either backend is required.
items.reference:
{"GET /products": "new",
 "POST /orders": "legacy"}

Why: the routing table is the single source of truth — flipping one entry is the whole migration mechanism for that route.

items.prompt: In the route lifecycle (legacy-only → shadow → migrated → retired), what distinguishes 'shadow' from 'migrated'?
choices: Nothing — they're the same state with different names
In shadow, the client still gets the legacy answer while the new system is only compared in the background; in migrated, the client's answer actually comes from the new system
Shadow means the route is disabled entirely
Migrated means the legacy code has already been deleted
items.explanation: Shadow is a zero-risk evidence-gathering stage — the client-visible answer never changes. Migrated is the point where the new system's answer actually reaches real users, which should only happen once shadow evidence supports it.
items.reference:
Legacy-only→Shadow→Migrated→Retired

Why: each state exists to gate risk — a route only advances once it has earned it with evidence.

items.prompt: A route sits in 'migrated' for months, fully served by the new system, but its legacy code path is still deployed and untouched. Is that route 'retired'?
choices: Yes — if traffic is fully on the new system, it's retired by definition
No — retirement is a separate, deliberate step (deleting the legacy code path), not something that happens automatically once traffic has moved
Yes, as long as it's been more than a week
No — a route can never be retired while the legacy system still exists at all
items.explanation: Migrated and retired are distinct states on purpose. A route can be fully migrated in traffic while its legacy implementation stays around as an untested rollback target — deleting that legacy code is a deliberate call made once enough migrated time has passed.
items.reference:
Legacy-only→Shadow→Migrated→Retired

Why: each state exists to gate risk — a route only advances once it has earned it with evidence.

items.prompt: A regression is found on a 'migrated' route. According to the lifecycle diagram, what's the valid next state?
choices: Retired — deleting the legacy code is the fix
Legacy-only — flip the route back until the regression is fixed
Shadow — the route must restart the entire evidence-gathering process from zero
The lifecycle has no path backward once a route is migrated
items.explanation: The lifecycle explicitly allows migrated → legacy-only as a direct move, which is exactly the fast rollback the facade is built for — no need to restart the full shadow evidence-gathering process for a route that had already proven itself before this regression.
items.reference:
Legacy-only→Shadow→Migrated→Retired

Why: each state exists to gate risk — a route only advances once it has earned it with evidence.

items.prompt: Why does the facade return the legacy response during shadowing instead of the new system's response, given both are already computed?
choices: Because computing the new system's response is only for logging, and returning it would require extra code
Because shadowing's purpose is gathering evidence before any customer depends on the new system — returning its answer would make a bug in it a real incident instead of a logged comparison
Because the legacy system is always faster to respond
There's no real reason — either response would work equally well
items.explanation: Returning the legacy answer keeps the blast radius at zero during the evidence-gathering stage. The moment the new system's answer reaches a real client, an undiscovered bug stops being a comparison-log entry and becomes an actual incident.
items.reference:
Shadow call: both systems run → client gets legacy answer → agreement is logged, not enforced.

Why: a bug in the new system stays inert until the route is actually flipped to 'new'.

items.prompt: A route's shadow match rate has been 100% for two weeks. Is that alone sufficient reason to flip it fully to the new system?
choices: Yes — 100% agreement means the new system is proven
Not by itself — it only proves agreement on the traffic that actually occurred; low-frequency inputs or unusual data the shadow period never saw are still unproven
No — shadowing can never justify a flip regardless of match rate
Yes, but only if the match rate was measured on a Friday
items.explanation: A high match rate over representative traffic is strong evidence, but it's still bounded by what traffic actually occurred during the window — it says nothing about paths that traffic hasn't exercised yet. The flip decision weighs that evidence against how costly an undiscovered gap would be for that specific route.
items.reference:
Shadow call: both systems run → client gets legacy answer → agreement is logged, not enforced.

Why: a bug in the new system stays inert until the route is actually flipped to 'new'.

items.prompt: Why is retiring (deleting) the legacy code path treated as a separate, deliberate step rather than something that happens automatically at 100% migrated traffic?
choices: It isn't — retirement should always happen the instant a route hits 100% new traffic
Because the legacy path still serves as a tested-in-production rollback target, and deleting it too early removes that safety net before enough migrated time has proven the new system stable
Legacy code can never actually be deleted, only disabled
Because deleting code always requires a full system rewrite
items.explanation: Keeping the legacy path around after a flip preserves the ability to roll back cheaply. Retirement gives that up in exchange for not maintaining dead code forever — a trade worth making only once enough time has passed to trust the new system without it.
items.reference:
100% traffic on 'new' ≠ retired. Legacy code stays as a rollback target until deliberately deleted.

Why: deleting legacy code too early removes the safety net before it's actually earned removal.

items.prompt: What happens if a team never retires any legacy code paths, even years after every route shows 'new' in the routing table?
choices: Nothing bad — it's strictly safer to keep the old code forever
It defeats the purpose of migrating at all — it just relocates the 'does anyone still understand this' problem instead of resolving it, while paying to maintain two systems indefinitely
The facade will eventually stop working
The legacy system will automatically delete itself after a fixed time
items.explanation: The whole point of the migration was to retire the legacy system's maintenance burden, not just stop sending it traffic. Never retiring anything keeps paying that cost indefinitely while gaining none of the simplification the migration was meant to deliver.
items.reference:
100% traffic on 'new' ≠ retired. Legacy code stays as a rollback target until deliberately deleted.

Why: deleting legacy code too early removes the safety net before it's actually earned removal.

items.prompt: What's a reasonable trigger for finally deleting a route's legacy code path?
choices: The moment its routing table entry first shows 'new'
After enough migrated time has passed that a regression would rather be fixed forward than rolled back to code nobody has touched in months
Exactly one calendar year after the project started, regardless of route
Only once every route in the entire system has migrated
items.explanation: The right trigger is confidence-based, not calendar-based or all-or-nothing: once enough time and evidence has accumulated that reverting to stale, unmaintained legacy code is no longer the preferred fix for a regression, that route's legacy path can be safely deleted independent of other routes.
items.reference:
100% traffic on 'new' ≠ retired. Legacy code stays as a rollback target until deliberately deleted.

Why: deleting legacy code too early removes the safety net before it's actually earned removal.

items.prompt: Implement `stableBucket(identity)` so it returns a deterministic integer between 0 and 99 for a given identity string. The same identity must always produce the same bucket — no `Math.random()` involved.

tests.description: same identity gives same bucket every call
different identities can give different buckets

items.explanation: A deterministic string hash (multiply-and-add over character codes, folded into a 32-bit int with `| 0`) followed by `% 100` gives a stable bucket with no external state and no per-call randomness — the same identity always lands in the same bucket, which is exactly what a rollout that shouldn't flip mid-session needs.
items.reference:
A random draw per request can put the same user on different systems within one session. A deterministic hash of identity fixes that.

Why: stability per identity, not per request, is what a real facade needs.

items.prompt: Implement `stableBucket(key)` returning a deterministic 0-99 integer for a string key, such that `stableBucket('a:x')` and `stableBucket('b:x')` are allowed to differ even though both contain `'x'` — the whole key matters, not just part of it.

tests.description: full key matters, not a substring

items.explanation: Hashing over every character of the full key (not a substring) means two keys that merely share a fragment, like both ending in ':x', still hash independently based on their complete content — this is what lets a route+identity composite key give each route its own independent bucket assignment for the same identity.
items.reference:
A random draw per request can put the same user on different systems within one session. A deterministic hash of identity fixes that.

Why: stability per identity, not per request, is what a real facade needs.

items.prompt: Given a `stableBucket(key)` function (already implemented, deterministic 0-99) and a route's `rolloutPercent` (0-100), implement `resolveTarget(bucket, rolloutPercent)` returning `'new'` if the bucket falls under the rollout percentage, else `'legacy'`. Treat `rolloutPercent <= 0` as always legacy and `>= 100` as always new.

tests.description: bucket under the percent is new
bucket at or above the percent is legacy

items.explanation: Comparing the identity's fixed bucket against the current rollout percentage gives a stable, gradually-widening slice of identities landing on 'new' as the percentage increases over time, while any single identity's answer never flips back and forth as long as the percentage itself doesn't change.
items.reference:
bucket < rolloutPercent ? 'new' : 'legacy'

Why: comparing a fixed bucket to a rising percentage gives a stable, gradually-widening rollout.

items.prompt: Implement `resolveTarget(config, bucket)` where `config` is `{ target: 'legacy' | 'new', rolloutPercent?: number }`. If `config.target === 'legacy'`, always return `'legacy'` regardless of rollout. Otherwise apply the rollout percentage against `bucket` the same way as a normal gradual rollout (undefined percent means fully 'new').

tests.description: target new with no rolloutPercent is fully new
target new with rolloutPercent respects the bucket

items.explanation: The route's own `target` field is checked first as a hard override — a route explicitly marked legacy should never be pulled toward 'new' by a stale rollout percentage left over from an earlier configuration. Only once `target === 'new'` does the percentage-based bucket comparison apply at all.
items.reference:
bucket < rolloutPercent ? 'new' : 'legacy'

Why: comparing a fixed bucket to a rising percentage gives a stable, gradually-widening rollout.

items.prompt: Given an array of shadow log entries `{ matched: boolean }`, implement `matchRate(log)` returning the fraction that matched, as a number between 0 and 1. Return `1` for an empty log (no evidence of mismatch yet).
items.explanation: Defaulting an empty log to a match rate of 1 avoids a misleading 0/0 division and correctly reflects that 'no evidence yet' is not the same claim as 'proven to disagree' — the dashboard number a team watches before raising a route's rollout percentage.
items.reference:
Match rate is the number watched before raising rolloutPercent — not 'passes tests', but 'agrees with production on production's own traffic'.

Why: this is a stricter, more honest bar than a test suite alone.

items.prompt: Given shadow log entries `{ path: string, matched: boolean }`, implement `matchRateForPath(log, path)` returning the match fraction restricted to entries for that `path` only. Return `1` if no entries exist for that path.

tests.description: filters to the given path only
computes fraction within the filtered path

items.explanation: A single shared log across all routes needs per-path filtering before computing a rate, since one route's high match rate shouldn't be diluted or hidden by another route's unrelated mismatches — each route earns its own rollout decision on its own evidence.
items.reference:
Match rate is the number watched before raising rolloutPercent — not 'passes tests', but 'agrees with production on production's own traffic'.

Why: this is a stricter, more honest bar than a test suite alone.

items.prompt: Given shadow log entries `{ matched: boolean }`, implement `mismatches(log)` returning only the entries where `matched` is `false`.
items.explanation: Every disagreement is a concrete, replayable bug report against the new system generated for free by traffic that would have happened anyway — surfacing exactly those entries is what lets a team investigate real gaps instead of just watching an aggregate rate.
items.reference:
Every mismatch is a free, real bug report — generated by traffic that would have happened anyway.

Why: surfacing individual disagreements is what makes a low match rate actionable, not just alarming.

items.prompt: Given shadow log entries `{ path: string, matched: boolean }`, implement `mismatchesForPath(log, path)` returning only the mismatched entries (`matched === false`) restricted to the given `path`.

tests.description: excludes matched entries even on the right path
empty when path has no entries

items.explanation: Combining both filters (path and matched===false) in one pass gives a route-scoped, actionable mismatch list — exactly what a team investigating one specific route's disagreements needs, without unrelated routes' mismatches mixed in.
items.reference:
Every mismatch is a free, real bug report — generated by traffic that would have happened anyway.

Why: surfacing individual disagreements is what makes a low match rate actionable, not just alarming.

items.prompt: Implement a `RoutingTable` with `setRoute(path, target)` and `getRoute(path)`. `getRoute` should return `'legacy'` as the default for any path never explicitly set.

tests.description: setRoute then getRoute returns the set value

items.explanation: Defaulting an unset route to 'legacy' means a brand-new route added to the codebase is automatically safe by default — it can't accidentally be served by an unproven new system just because nobody has explicitly configured it yet.
items.reference:
An unconfigured route must default to 'legacy' — safety by default, not by omission.

Why: a new route nobody has explicitly migrated should never accidentally land on unproven code.

items.prompt: Implement `pickBackend(routes, path, legacyBackend, newBackend)` where `routes` is a plain object mapping path to `'legacy' | 'new'`. Return `newBackend` only if `routes[path] === 'new'` exactly; return `legacyBackend` for every other case, including an unset path.
items.explanation: Checking for the exact string `'new'` rather than treating any truthy value as 'new' avoids a subtle bug where an unexpected value (a typo, `undefined`, or some other string) would silently route to the new system instead of failing safe to legacy.
items.reference:
An unconfigured route must default to 'legacy' — safety by default, not by omission.

Why: a new route nobody has explicitly migrated should never accidentally land on unproven code.

items.prompt: Implement `isSafeToShadow(method)` returning `true` for HTTP methods that are safe to call on both legacy and new systems during shadowing without a real side effect (`'GET'`, `'HEAD'`), and `false` for methods that mutate state (`'POST'`, `'PUT'`, `'DELETE'`, `'PATCH'`).
items.explanation: Read-only methods can be called against the new system for free comparison, since they have no side effects to worry about duplicating. Mutating methods can't be shadowed the same naive way — calling a real POST against the new system would actually create a second order, so those routes need a different strategy (a sandboxed copy of the new system, or skipping shadowing in favor of a small rollout percentage with fast rollback).
items.reference:
GET/HEAD: safe to call twice, no side effect. POST/PUT/DELETE/PATCH: calling both systems for real would double the side effect.

Why: shadowing a write route naively duplicates the write — it needs a different strategy than a read route.

items.prompt: Implement `needsCompensatingAction(method, alreadyExecutedOnNew)` returning `true` only when the route is a mutating method (`'POST'`, `'PUT'`, `'DELETE'`, `'PATCH'`) AND it already executed on the new system before a rollback — meaning flipping the route back to legacy alone won't undo the effect. Return `false` for a read method or when nothing has executed yet.

tests.description: POST not yet executed needs no compensation

items.explanation: Flipping a routing table entry back to 'legacy' is safe for GET by construction, since nothing was ever created or changed. It is not automatically safe for a POST that already charged a card or wrote a row on the new system — routing the next request to legacy doesn't undo what the previous one already did, which is exactly why mutating routes need a compensating action defined before they're migrated, not improvised mid-incident.
items.reference:
GET/HEAD: safe to call twice, no side effect. POST/PUT/DELETE/PATCH: calling both systems for real would double the side effect.

Why: shadowing a write route naively duplicates the write — it needs a different strategy than a read route.
